presentingComplaint: Cough for 6 weeks with blood-streaked sputum, unintentional weight loss, and evening fevers with night sweats
history: 52-year-old man, works as a daily-wage construction laborer, presents with a productive cough for 6 weeks, initially dry, now with scant blood-streaked sputum for the last 4-5 days. He describes low-grade fever most afternoons/evenings with drenching night sweats, and has lost approximately 6 kg over the past 2 months with progressive anorexia and fatigue. He reports mild exertional breathlessness but no chest pain. No prior TB treatment. He mentions a paternal uncle was treated for 'chest TB' about a year ago and they shared living quarters for several months. No known HIV status (never tested), no diabetes, non-smoker, occasional alcohol use, no IV drug use. No recent travel outside India. No prior hospitalization or antibiotic use in the last 90 days.
examination: Thin, chronically ill-appearing man in no acute distress. Mild pallor. No icterus, no lymphadenopathy. Chest: reduced breath sounds and coarse crepitations over the right upper zone posteriorly; no wheeze. Cardiovascular and abdominal exam unremarkable, no hepatosplenomegaly. No focal neurological deficit.
imaging: Chest X-ray: cavitary lesion in the right upper lobe with surrounding fibronodular infiltrates and volume loss
microbiology: Sputum CBNAAT (Xpert MTB/RIF): Mycobacterium tuberculosis detected, rifampicin resistance not detected
contraindications: Avoid empirical fluoroquinolone monotherapy before excluding TB in a patient with a compatible chronic respiratory syndrome, as this can partially treat TB, delay diagnosis, and promote fluoroquinolone-resistant TB
Confirm HIV status before initiating anti-TB therapy given implications for regimen/duration and ART interaction
edgeCases: If sputum AFB/CBNAAT were negative despite high clinical suspicion, would require further evaluation (repeat sputum, bronchoscopy with BAL, or empirical anti-TB therapy in high-prevalence settings per NTEP algorithm)
Hemoptysis in this setting should also prompt exclusion of secondary aspergilloma within an old TB cavity if symptoms persist after treatment
This case represents an infectious/granulomatous disease rather than an acute bacterial syndrome; not part of the acute sepsis/CAP severity scoring pathway
expectedMaiK: MaiK should flag chronic cough (>=2 weeks) with constitutional symptoms (weight loss, night sweats, evening fever) and cavitatory imaging as classic for pulmonary TB, prompting sputum AFB/CBNAAT and airborne isolation rather than empirical antibacterial therapy.
expectedNextQuestions: Any prior anti-TB treatment (to assess for drug resistance risk)
Contact tracing details and screening of household contacts
Assessment of hemoptysis severity and need for further imaging (CT chest) if it worsens
expectedInvestigations: Sputum culture with drug susceptibility testing
CT chest (if diagnosis unclear or complications suspected)
